findings.headline: Deskilling or replacement, and production access: on the pages checked, every option asserts and none shows proof. Investigations and Rootly make the strictest promises on access.
findings.short: Engineers worry that AI incident tools will deskill or replace them, and about what those tools can touch in production. On the pages checked, none of the 6 options shows proof on either.
findings.title: No option answers two common worries with proof yet
findings.explain: Beyond whether the AI works, engineers worry about what it does to them and to their systems. The model counts 33 posts worrying that these tools will deskill or replace engineers, and 23 wary of giving an AI access to production systems or data. On the pages checked, every option makes claims on both, and none shows proof.
findings.note: The model counts 33 deskilling or replacement posts and 23 on access. Claude then read each in full: 14 of the 33 are squarely about AI tools deskilling or replacing engineers, and 14 are related (skills lost to AI-written code, who is accountable, or the trade-off mentioned in passing). The rest don't fit. 20 of the 23 access posts fit.
findings.implication: On deskilling, incident.io's launch post says you and the agent work the problem together, with its reasoning shown, and its Nexus page says it raises the floor for new hires. Nobody shows responders keeping or building their skills; Datadog comes closest, with one named customer saying newer engineers now begin with a head start, and another that it could raise skill levels. Evidence of what on-call engineers learn from its reasoning would be the first on this row. On access, incident.io's product page says Investigations' only change is a pull request you review, as strict a promise as Rootly's sign-off on every change. To turn that promise into proof, it could show exactly what Investigations can read, with which permissions, and how “pull request only” is enforced.
findings.whyRanked: It is the less obvious concern, it outweighs wrong-cause complaints since 2025 in this data, and incident.io's claims only assert a position with no proof.

quotes.quote: Even if an engineer reads the output of the AI and understands the root cause of the problems and how to diagnose the incident, somehow it's hard for them to internalize the learning and apply it next time to a new incident.
What makes "read-only" a guarantee rather than a convention? In Python a plain attribute read can hit a @property that lazy-loads from the DB; in Java a getter can mutate state or take a lock.

findings.headline: 73 of 430 posts use or recommend a general AI tool for incident work, 49 of them positive about it; only 8 of those 73 argue that makes a dedicated product unnecessary.
findings.title: Many engineers already use a general AI tool for incident work
findings.explain: 73 of the 430 posts describe using or recommending a general AI tool, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor, for incident work, and 49 of them are positive about it. Only 8 of those 73 argue that this makes a dedicated product unnecessary. So it is less an objection than a habit, but it makes the tool they already use the likely yardstick for Investigations.
findings.implication: incident.io argues on its blog that in-house builds rarely measure accuracy, and ships a plugin for the agents engineers already use. Its product page says it backtests Investigations daily against real past incidents, and its blog says it freezes each incident in time so every new version runs on exactly the same inputs, grading each hypothesis on a published scale from a bullseye to a miss. What's missing is a published score from those tests, and the same test run on a general agent given the same access. Saying how the incidents are chosen would let sceptics judge the test, not just the score. A score across many incidents needn't reveal any customer's data.
findings.whyRanked: It answers the do-it-yourself question directly: the behaviour is real, the stated objection is rare, and incident.io's own coverage here is only anecdote.

quotes.quote: I also encouraged my team to paste any inquiries or alerts we got in our slack channel verbatim into codex and follow that procedure until it could figure it out as a one-shot.

findings.headline: 50 of 430 posts say the AI gets the cause wrong or that its reasoning can't be checked.
findings.title: Engineers will ask how often it's wrong
findings.explain: 50 posts say the AI gets the cause wrong, or that its reasoning can't be checked. incident.io's pages show proof on both. On the pages checked, the only other option with proof that its reasoning can be checked is one engineer's do-it-yourself write-up.
findings.implication: The proof so far is a measured jump in accurate early updates, and an incident write-up in which its conclusion was checked against the code. Each customer can see its own accuracy on its Investigations homepage, and incident.io's buyer's guide tells evaluators to ask vendors for accuracy figures (precision and recall). No option on the map publishes them yet. A score from the daily backtests described above would give buyers the figure its own guide tells them to ask for.
findings.whyRanked: It is well supported by the data but familiar, and incident.io already has proof on these objections, so the gain is in how it shows misses.
